clue.text: Californian intended to have fun here before I do?

definitions.text: Californian intended to have fun here before I do?

blocks.clueFragment: Californian intended to have fun here
blocks.note: the surface reads as a Californian who plans to enjoy himself somewhere
the setter means a noun: one's intended is a fiancé, and 'I do' is his wedding vow, so this is his last night out, named the American way

explanation.surface: Someone from California announces plans for a good time before getting round to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intended' looks like a verb and is the husband-to-be. 'Californian' asks for the American name; the British call it a stag do.
explanation.definitionFit: The celebration an American groom has with friends on the eve of his wedding vows goes by exactly this name.

clue.text: Bouncers sitting around until queue’s like this?

indicators.note: people sitting around a thing surround it

blocks.note: in cricket a bouncer, a short ball rearing up at the batsman, is also called a bumper
until = to, as in 'nine to five'
the plural supplies a second one to close the sandwich

explanation.surface: Nightclub doormen lounging about until a queue forms outside.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'Bouncers' supplies both BUMPERs, one either side of TO. Nightclub bouncers are the false trail; the cricket sense is the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic stuck nose to tail in a jam has each car's front almost touching the rear of the car ahead.

clue.text: Clergy‘s fate in its traditional environment

indicators.note: one thing sits in another

blocks.note: the clergy's traditional home is the church, abbreviated CH
one's lot is one's fate

explanation.surface: A reflection on what becomes of priests in their customary setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its' points back at the clergy, whose traditional setting is the church, CH.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The cloth' is an idiom for priests and ministers collectively, from their distinctive clerical dress.

clue.text: Leader of EU introducing plan to link with India and China in particular

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the bloc's initials is taken

blocks.note: the first letter of EU
spec, short for specification, is a plan or design
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet
china plate is rhyming slang for mate, and a mate is an ally

explanation.surface: The head of the European Union unveils a scheme to build ties with two Asian powers.
explanation.walkthrough: China here is not the country: in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, so a china is a friend or ally.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs singling out one item above the others, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Left out pud scoffed by rabbit with head down

indicators.note: in a down entry the head is the top
food scoffed by an animal ends up inside it

blocks.note: a doe is a female rabbit
pud is an old word for a hand or paw, and so is mitt

explanation.surface: A rabbit gobbles a pudding that was left out, then hangs its head.
explanation.walkthrough: Pud looks like pudding, but it is an old dialect word for a hand or paw. In a down entry the head is the top letter, so dropping it moves it to the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Something omitted has been missed out or excluded, a plain synonym of the past participle phrase.

clue.text: Member of the Greens further in lead?

blocks.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead, from Latin plumbum
further = other, additional, as in 'further reasons'

explanation.surface: Asks whether a Green Party politician is edging ahead in the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital G makes the Greens look like the political party; they are leafy vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant grown for its leaves to cook, such as spinach or chard, belongs among the green vegetables.

clue.text: Composer’s unfinished fanfare

indicators.note: work left unfinished stops short

blocks.note: Maurice Ravel, French composer of Boléro

explanation.surface: A composer's fanfare was never completed.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining wordplay to definition. Fanfare here is figurative: a burst of praise, not trumpets.
explanation.definitionFit: A rave review is enthusiastic praise, and a fanfare figuratively means a showy public celebration of something.

clue.text: Body of water moving slowly across English Channel some say

indicators.note: letters that are moving do not stay put

blocks.note: anagram fodder
E = English
ea is a dialect word for a river or drainage channel, found in the Fens

explanation.surface: A body of water drifts sluggishly over the English Channel, or so people claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English Channel' wants to be the sea between England and France; it splits into E and a dialect word for a drain. The anagram of SLOWLY takes the E in its second slot.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea between China and Korea is a named marine body of water, so it fits the general description.

clue.text: One of the people with reservations after organising a race in Vietnam

definitions.text: One of the people with reservations

indicators.note: organising puts things into a new arrangement, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: Someone with doubts about staging a running event in Southeast Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People with reservations' sounds like doubters; the reservations are tribal lands set aside in the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Many indigenous tribes in the United States live on or govern reservations, lands held for them by treaty.

clue.text: It hasn’t been decided if option with only half of motion is resolved

indicators.note: keeping only half of a six-letter word leaves its front three letters
to resolve something is to break it down and reorganise it, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: anagram fodder
the first half of the six-letter word motion

explanation.surface: A committee debates whether a half-passed motion counts as settled.
explanation.walkthrough: The meeting-room vocabulary of option, motion and resolved keeps the reader thinking of procedure rather than letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A question still open to debate, with no settled conclusion, is exactly what people call this phrase.

clue.text: Bad guy drops in house …

blocks.note: a villain is the bad guy of a story
the letters that get dropped

explanation.surface: A villain pays a visit, dropping in at someone's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops in' reads as a casual visit; split it, and 'in' is the chunk removed. The ellipsis carries the definition on into the next clue: a house in Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: A large country residence, especially an ancient Roman one, is called by this name.

clue.text: … in Rome, and here’s right thing to do

indicators.note: tells the solver to put the next words into Latin, the language of Rome

blocks.note: et is Latin for and
hic is Latin for here, and the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: Continues the villain's visit: when in Rome, here is how to behave.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to the house before, but 'in Rome' also works on its own, as the instruction to translate into Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral principle guides how a person ought to behave, telling them the proper course of action.

clue.text: Journey by plane, possibly leaving trailer park at last

indicators.note: a trailer is what trails at the back
points to the final letter of the word just before it

blocks.note: a plane is a tree, and TREE leaving its trailer loses its final E
the last letter of parK

explanation.surface: Someone flies off, leaving their caravan behind at the holiday park.
explanation.walkthrough: The plane is not an aircraft but the plane tree, common in London streets; 'possibly' marks it as one example of a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, arduous trip, often made on foot, is a common synonym for a journey.

clue.text: Bear stretcher

blocks.note: the cartoon bear of Jellystone Park, friend of Boo-Boo
a practitioner of yoga spends the time stretching

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear stretcher' sounds like something to carry a wounded bear on. 'Stretcher' is one who stretches.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous cartoon bear bears this name, and a yoga practitioner is someone who holds long body stretches.

clue.text: Cheers to support artist embroiled in country music drama

indicators.note: someone embroiled in something is caught up inside it
in a down entry a support sits underneath

blocks.note: the Baltic country
RA = Royal Academician, a crossword's usual artist
ta is British slang for thanks, like cheers

explanation.surface: Applause for a performer caught up in a Nashville-style row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country music' looks like one phrase, but country is LATVIA and music drama the definition. Cheers and ta are both British for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's opera about the courtesan Violetta is a sung stage work, which is what an opera is.

clue.text: Sculptress gets royal household to back mammoth features reduced by 40 per cent

indicators.note: two fifths of a five-letter word is two letters, so the plural loses its last pair
to back something is to come behind it

blocks.clueFragment: mammoth features reduced by 40 per cent
blocks.note: a mammoth's features are its TUSKS, cut from five letters to three
the House of Saud, the royal family of Saudi Arabia

explanation.surface: A sculptor wins royal backing for a scaled-down mammoth.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Tussaud modelled wax figures, now the London museum. The royal household is a dynasty, not the Windsors.
explanation.definitionFit: Marie Tussaud was a wax modeller whose portrait figures founded the famous museum bearing her surname.

clue.text: Tickets you all but lost for club

indicators.note: all but means everything except one piece, so the word drops its final letter
something lost has gone astray, so these letters wander out of their order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
YOU without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone mislaid nearly all the tickets for a night at the club.
explanation.walkthrough: Stoke City is an English football club from Stoke-on-Trent. The surface points at a nightclub.
explanation.definitionFit: A professional football team from the Potteries is known as a club, the normal British word for such teams.

clue.text: Sound of loud club

blocks.note: brassy = loud and brash

explanation.surface: The noise coming from a loud nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: The club is a golf club: an old name for the two-wood, once soled with brass.
explanation.definitionFit: An old golfing term for the wooden-headed number two wood, one of the sticks in a player's bag.

clue.text: How criminals run much of Italy?

blocks.note: to run liquor is to smuggle it, the Prohibition-era trade
split 4,3, the map shows Italy as a boot on a leg

explanation.surface: A question about how the mafia controls most of the Italian peninsula.
explanation.walkthrough: Run means smuggle, as in rum-running. The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: Italy's outline is a boot and leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Illegally made or smuggled goods, especially alcohol during Prohibition, are described with this adjective or verb.

clue.text: Venetian fare‘s good – not so tiny quantity welcome!

blocks.note: G = good
no is the answer to 'is it so?' when it is not
cc = cubic centimetre, a small volume
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A diner rates the Venetian food as good but the portions far too small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so' reads as 'not very' but is a flat denial, NO.
explanation.definitionFit: Potato dumplings are a staple dish of northern Italian cooking, Venice included, so they are regional food.

clue.text: Bitter commentary when broadcasting endless massacre

indicators.note: without an end, the word that follows loses its last letter
broadcasting scatters things widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: MASSACRE with its final E removed, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A cutting remark about news bulletins that never stop reporting slaughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcasting' fits the news surface and is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocking or cutting remarks meant to wound are a form of acid, scornful speech.

clue.text: One following ballsy cooking programmes

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are mixed up
one follows the other words, so it goes at the end

blocks.note: anagram fodder
I = one

explanation.surface: A fan tuning in to bold, brash cookery shows on television.
explanation.walkthrough: The programmes are not television but courses of study.
explanation.definitionFit: A course outline sets out what will be taught, like a programme of study, and this is its plural.

clue.text: Qualified for several races

blocks.note: qualified as an adjective: fit or proper, an archaic sense from the prayer book
an athletics fixture with many races on one programme

explanation.surface: An athlete has qualified to run in several heats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Qualified' reads as a verb; it is an adjective meaning suitable, the old sense of meet, as in 'meet and right'.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adjective means suitable or fitting, and the noun names a sports gathering of many events.

clue.text: Dismiss British Member of Parliament

blocks.note: B = British
a group of owls is called a parliament, so an owl is one member

explanation.surface: A call to sack a British politician.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bowler dismisses a batsman by bowling him. 'Member of Parliament' is not an MP but a bird: parliament is the collective noun for owls.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, when the ball hits the stumps the batsman is out, the bowler having sent him back.

clue.text: Substitute sex drive with this

blocks.note: sex is Latin for six, VI in Roman numerals
what you drive

explanation.surface: Advice to channel one's libido into something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex drive' is one phrase in the surface and two parts in the wordplay; sex is the Latin word for six, continuing the Latin theme of 11 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The word derives from Latin vicarius, a deputy, and the dictionary still gives stand-in or delegate as a meaning.

clue.text: Company in Italy’s source of fur

blocks.note: Co. = company
at = in, as in 'at home'
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A firm in Italy supplies furs to the fashion trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction but simply gives AT.
explanation.definitionFit: A raccoon-like mammal of the Americas with a ringed tail has a pelt that can be taken as fur.

clue.text: Focus lost in difficult dance move

indicators.note: the focus of a word is its central letter, and here that centre is lost

blocks.note: a steep climb is a difficult one

explanation.surface: A dancer loses concentration during a tricky routine.
explanation.walkthrough: STEEP has five letters, so its focus is the central E, the third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A single movement of the feet in a dance routine is called by this name.

clue.text: Dislodge string found aboard Nelson’s flagship?

indicators.note: a string of letters found aboard the ship lies inside its name, so the outer letters are shed

blocks.note: Nelson's flagship at Trafalgar was HMS Victory, known as the Victory

explanation.surface: A piece of rope turns up on HMS Victory and gets pulled loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'String' means a string of letters, not rope. The question mark warns that the ship's name, the Victory, must be supplied before the hidden run appears.
explanation.definitionFit: To force a tenant out of a home is to remove or oust them, a synonym for forcing them from place.

clue.text: Coach group from SA stuck behind chestnut horse

blocks.note: ch is the stud-book abbreviation for a chestnut horse
an Arab is a breed of horse
the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

explanation.surface: A tour party from South Africa trapped behind a horse on a country lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chestnut horse' reads as one animal but gives two parts: CH, the colour abbreviation, and the ARAB.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned open motor bus used for day trips, once common in Britain, is a kind of coach.

clue.text: Absolutely irrational adult with made-up story about how to appeal to the young and wealthy?

definitions.text: how to appeal to the young and wealthy?

blocks.note: yup = yes, absolutely
pi is an irrational number
fiction is invented narrative
A = adult, the film certificate

explanation.surface: A cynical view of marketing that tells wealthy young people absurd stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irrational' looks like an adjective for the adult; in maths pi is an irrational number.
explanation.definitionFit: Remaking a neighbourhood or product to attract young urban professionals is a process named after those yuppies.
